job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A)—threshold and single-vessel limit.** The definition covers recovery only when a *single vessel* exceeds 10,000 metric tons in a year. An operator could stay below the threshold per vessel—or divide operations among vessels or years—and argue that commercial mining is not covered.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—depth and resource scope.** The 200-meter cutoff excludes activity in shallower seabed areas, and “polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources” does not clearly cover every form of seabed extraction or associated processing. Those gaps could invite disputes over whether particular deposits, depths, or activities qualify.

3. **Section 2(1)(B)—unclear risk standard.** The Secretary’s authority to decide what poses “comparable” ecosystem risks has no criteria, process, or deadline. That invites inconsistent decisions and legal challenges, and leaves the prohibition’s scope uncertain.

4. **Section 2(2)—narrow U.S.-person definition.** The definition includes citizens and corporations organized under state law, but does not clearly cover U.S. residents who are not citizens, partnerships, LLCs, or other entities. It also does not expressly reach foreign subsidiaries or entities controlled by U.S. persons, allowing potential evasion through organizational structures.

5. **Section 2(3)—covered-vessel limits.** Registration applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons that are “equipped” for recovery. Smaller vessels, vessels not readily characterized as equipped, and multi-vessel operations may fall outside the registry, even if they support mining covered by section 3.

6. **Section 3(a)—jurisdictional gap.** The prohibition reaches persons “in the United States” and U.S. persons anywhere, but does not clearly reach foreign persons conducting mining wholly outside the United States. It also leaves uncertain whether a person’s presence in the United States must coincide with the prohibited conduct.

7. **Section 3(a)—“engage in” is undefined.** The bill does not say whether arranging, financing, transporting, processing, or knowingly assisting mining counts as engaging in it. Companies could argue that their supporting activities are outside the prohibition.

8. **Section 3(b)—existing-operations exemption.** Mining under any exploration license issued before enactment is exempt, with no end date, limits on the amount or location of mining, or requirement that the license be valid and in good standing. An exploration license could therefore be used to continue commercial extraction indefinitely.

9. **Section 3(c)—environmental-assessment exemption.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” is undefined and has no limits on scale, duration, or commercial recovery. An operator could characterize extraction as assessment work, and the text does not clearly prevent sale or use of minerals recovered under the exemption.

10. **Sections 3 and 4—no clear link between registry and prohibition.** The registry does not require approval, and registration does not appear to establish compliance with section 3. Conversely, the prohibition is not limited to registered vessels, leaving unclear how the registry is meant to support enforcement.

11. **Section 4(a)—no registration deadline or complete coverage.** The bill does not say when registration is due, what information must be supplied, or whether registration is required before a vessel is equipped or operated. It also requires registration only for covered vessels, leaving potentially relevant smaller vessels untracked.

12. **Section 4(b)—weak reporting requirements.** Reports need only describe “recovery activities,” without specifying locations, quantities, methods, or related environmental impacts; quarterly reporting could also leave long gaps. The bill provides no verification or audit authority and no express consequence for failing to report or submitting false information.

13. **Section 4—undefined operator and responsible parties.** “Operator” is not defined, and the bill does not clarify which entity is responsible when ownership, operation, and control are divided among companies. That could make registration and reporting obligations difficult to enforce against the responsible party.

14. **Section 5(a)—penalty ambiguity and limits.** “Not more than $1,000,000” leaves the penalty amount and factors for setting it unspecified, while “each day” does not clarify how continuing or multiple violations are counted. The provision also does not identify the enforcing agency or provide procedures for assessing, reviewing, or collecting penalties.

15. **Section 5(b)—criminal enforcement uncertainty.** The bill does not specify which officials may bring criminal cases or clarify how willfulness applies to corporate entities and continuing violations. That can complicate enforcement and create disputes over the required state of mind.

16. **Sections 5 and 8—penalties may reach pre-effective-date conduct.** Section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days, but section 5(a) expressly applies to violations occurring on or after enactment. Because the prohibition is not yet effective during that interval, the penalty language risks imposing liability for conduct that was not yet prohibited.

17. **Section 6—no guarantee of an agreement.** The Secretary need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement; the bill does not require an agreement to be concluded, set milestones, or address what happens if negotiations fail. This provision therefore does not ensure equivalent international prohibitions.

18. **Section 7(a)—unclear standard and mechanism for ending the prohibition.** “Without serious harm” is undefined, and the bill does not specify what the National Academies report must assess or when it must be prepared. The phrase “Congress … finds by joint resolution” also leaves the legal effect unclear; a joint resolution generally must be enacted through the ordinary legislative process to change the law.

19. **Section 7(b)—conflict with the duration provision.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains in effect until Congress makes a specified finding, but section 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. The sunset can therefore lift the prohibition without the finding or assessment contemplated in subsection (a).

20. **Sections 3(b), 6, and 7—unclear timing anchors.** The existing-operations exception and penalty language use enactment as a reference point, while the prohibition takes effect 180 days later; the international-agreement deadline and sunset also run from enactment. The bill should state clearly how these dates interact, particularly whether licenses issued during the 180-day delay qualify for the exemption.
